target: AG1’s claim that AI makes everyday life more enjoyable and convenient, improves health and standard of living, makes work easier, helps people with disabilities, and improves workplace safety, leading to the conclusion that AI is good for society.
objection: AI can automate or replicate human work in ways that reduce labor demand and shift value toward owners of the technology, which can harm the economic well-being of many workers and businesses.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI’s benefits outweigh its harms for students and adults.
objection: When people rely on AI outputs for answers and decisions, it can weaken independent reasoning and reduce learning of underlying concepts, so AI can undermine critical thinking skills.

target: AG1’s positive view of AI’s social impact.
objection: Because AI models learn from biased data, they can reproduce or amplify discriminatory patterns in predictions and recommendations, harming racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism.

target: AG1’s positive view of AI’s social impact.
objection: AI systems often require collecting, linking, and processing personal or sensitive data, so they pose dangerous privacy risks.

target: AG1’s claim that responsible development and governance can substantially reduce AI’s main harms.
objection: Many AI harms stem from structural features of AI at scale—such as automation incentives, biased training data, and large-scale data collection—so substantial, society-wide elimination of those harms is not realistically achievable just by governance measures.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards can substantially mitigate the harms from AI.
objection: Auditing, privacy-preserving techniques, human oversight, worker transition support, and educational scaffolding may reduce some harms, but they do not remove the underlying structural drivers across all deployments and time horizons, so the harms persist at meaningful levels.

target: AG1’s view that AI’s benefits outweigh its harms.
objection: The harms to economic well-being, critical thinking, racial equality, and privacy are socially important because they directly affect opportunities, autonomy, and civil rights, so persistent harms can outweigh AI’s welfare gains.

target: AG1’s conclusion that AI can be good for society because it has benefits and some harms may remain.
objection: In real-world deployment, AI combines persistent harms with unevenly distributed benefits, so if harms are not adequately mitigated and benefits are concentrated, AI cannot be expected to be good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s welfare gains can outweigh risks and lead to net positive social outcomes.
objection: AI may create convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety gains, but those benefits do not automatically neutralize harms like displacement, discrimination, and privacy loss at a society-wide scale.

target: AG1’s implication that mitigation will make harms non-dominant.
objection: In practice, mitigation is uneven and cannot be assumed to fully eliminate labor disruption, discrimination, or privacy harms across all contexts and time horizons.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily concentrates market power because frontier compute and data are needed to participate meaningfully.
objection: AI development and deployment do not require every firm to own frontier compute or data pipelines; open models, pretrained tools, and cloud APIs can lower barriers to entry so competitive entry remains viable.

target: AG1’s conclusion that lowered barriers mean AI benefits will be broadly shared and broad economic harm is unlikely.
objection: If competitive entry remains viable, AI benefits are more likely to be distributed across many firms and customers rather than accruing only to dominant firms, reducing the likelihood of broad economic harm.

target: AG1’s claim that broad welfare gains across health, safety, accessibility, and productivity are enough to support that AI is good for society overall.
objection: Even if AI creates substantial welfare gains in major domains, whether it is good for society should be judged by overall welfare and quality of life, not only by the economic leverage of workers and small businesses.

target: AG1’s claim that broad welfare gains can offset concentration-related losses.
objection: Lowering barriers to build AI applications does not by itself prevent winner-take-most outcomes when dominant firms control key bottlenecks such as distribution, major customer access, and cheap large-scale deployment infrastructure.

target: AG1’s claim that competitive entry prevents concentration and broadens benefits.
objection: Even if many developers can build AI apps, winner-take-most concentration can still occur because dominant firms may capture value through bottlenecks that remain centralized.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits are broadly shared enough to offset economic losses.
objection: When dominance persists through concentrated value-capture bottlenecks, welfare gains are less likely to translate into broad gains for workers and smaller businesses, while displacement and leverage losses still fall widely.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy concerns do not decisively imply AI is not good overall when strong protections exist.
objection: Effective AI deployment typically requires collecting, linking, and processing personal or sensitive data at scale, which tends to increase the amount of personal data held and interconnected across the AI ecosystem.

target: AG1’s view that competition and privacy-preserving practices can keep privacy risks low.
objection: Competition among AI providers can intensify data-collection and data-sharing pressure because providers have incentives to collect more data to improve model performance, personalization, and retention.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks can be largely avoided or reliably compensated in practice.
objection: As the scale and linkability of personal data increase, privacy leakage and harmful inference become more likely and harder for any single actor to prevent across a wider ecosystem, so privacy risks persist at meaningful levels even with competitive entry.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s welfare gains can offset privacy objections.
objection: Significant privacy harms undermine autonomy and equal participation because people can be surveilled or adversely affected based on inferences about them, so these harms count strongly against AI overall.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks do not decisively show AI is not good for society overall.
objection: AG1’s welfare gains do not automatically show that high-stakes privacy harms are largely avoided or outweighed, so the conclusion that AI is socially beneficial is not established.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving methods and legal/contractual remedies can make privacy harms manageable.
objection: AI deployment often increases the amount of personal data held and interconnected, and even with privacy controls or remedies, privacy leakage and harmful inference can remain a meaningful societal risk.

target: AG1’s claim that effective privacy controls show privacy risks do not persist at meaningful levels across competitive AI deployments.
objection: Privacy risks can still persist across the AI ecosystem because the scale and linkability of personal data make downstream misuse difficult to fully prevent.

target: AG2’s claim that substantial, society-wide elimination of AI harms is not realistically achievable just by governance measures.
objection: Responsible development and governance—such as fairness auditing, privacy-preserving techniques, access controls, human-in-the-loop oversight, worker transition support, and educational scaffolding—can substantially reduce the main harm mechanisms cited by AG2.

target: AG2’s assumption that because harms cannot be perfectly eliminated, they dominate the overall impact.
objection: Whether AI is good for society should be judged by net impact on welfare and quality of life, not by whether it eliminates every risk perfectly, so the inability to remove every harm does not by itself show AI is not good overall.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot be good overall if some harms persist at meaningful levels.
objection: AI can produce meaningful welfare gains in everyday life, health, work, accessibility, and safety, and persistent risks can coexist with a net positive social effect when those gains are substantial.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI’s harms necessarily outweigh its benefits for society overall.
objection: AI’s strongest benefits include accessibility for people with disabilities, improvements in health information and service support, and workplace safety support, so its welfare gains can reach groups often at risk of exclusion or harm.

target: AG2’s concentration-based economic harm argument.
objection: Widely available AI tools such as pretrained/open models and cloud APIs can lower barriers for startups and independent developers, so winner-take-most concentration of AI power is not inevitable.

target: AG2’s claim that AI-driven concentration broadly harms economic well-being.
objection: If competitive entry remains viable, AI benefits are more likely to be distributed across many firms and customers, which weakens the claim that AI systematically causes broad economic harm across the board.

target: AG2’s emphasis on workers’ and small businesses’ economic leverage as the key criterion for judging AI.
objection: Whether AI is good for society should be evaluated by overall welfare and quality of life across multiple major domains, not only by economic leverage of workers and small businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that broad welfare gains do not imply good social outcomes when concentration persists.
objection: Many AI-enabled tools are available through common consumer and workplace channels rather than being captured only by dominant firms, so welfare improvements can be broadly shared rather than confined to frontier AI owners.

target: AG2’s claim that persistent concentration means AI’s benefits are not broadly shared enough to offset harms.
objection: Broadly shared welfare gains in health, safety, accessibility, and productivity/learning can offset some negative economic effects from concentration for many people in aggregate.

target: AG2’s weak_negation assumption that there is no evidence broad welfare gains offset broad economic losses.
objection: There is evidence that broadly shared welfare gains can offset widespread economic losses, so the assumption that no such evidence exists is false.

target: AG2’s claim that AI tends to intensify privacy risks even in competitive markets.
objection: Privacy-preserving deployment methods such as differential privacy, federated learning, on-device inference, and strict data minimization can prevent or greatly limit sensitive information inference when properly implemented.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks persist at meaningful levels across society despite competition.
objection: Many AI deployments use privacy-preserving practices and operate under legal or contractual enforcement that deters harmful data handling and provides remedies after misuse, showing privacy leakage and inference can be effectively prevented at scale in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks necessarily persist at meaningful levels across competitive AI deployments.
objection: If effective privacy controls and remedies are in place, then privacy leakage and harmful inference are not inevitable and the claim that privacy risks persist at meaningful levels across society is not warranted as a general conclusion.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s welfare gains do not outweigh privacy concerns.
objection: AI can still be socially beneficial when deployed with strong privacy protections, so privacy concerns do not decisively imply that AI is not good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that welfare gains from AI do not suffice because labor-market harms spill into health and safety.
objection: AI can improve health, safety, and productivity directly, and those gains can improve day-to-day well-being and reduce real harms for many non-dominant users.

target: AG2’s claim that AI tends to increase economic insecurity and thus worsen health and safety outcomes.
objection: AI can make work easier by reducing routine effort and supporting learning/productivity, which can improve workers’ and students’ economic prospects rather than only creating insecurity.

target: AG2’s claim that welfare gains are insufficient because they do not reach enough people.
objection: AI can broaden participation and opportunity for marginalized groups, including people with disabilities, so its welfare gains can reach groups that otherwise face exclusion.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits can offset concentration-related losses and make AI good overall.
objection: Economic insecurity from job displacement, wage suppression, and weakened bargaining power can worsen health and safety outcomes through stress, reduced resources for care, and unsafe conditions, so welfare gains in health/work/safety do not suffice to show AI is good overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s benefits can offset concentration-related losses.
objection: When bargaining power and alternatives shrink, workers and small firms face greater economic insecurity, so AI tends to increase insecurity for many workers and small businesses.

target: AG1’s sufficiency claim that health, work, safety, accessibility, and productivity gains are enough for an overall positive assessment.
objection: If AI increases economic insecurity for many workers and small businesses, it can also worsen health and safety outcomes, so the same welfare domains AG1 cites can be harmed by AI-related labor-market effects.
